notes.meaning: Joash was only seven years old when he became king of Judah, and he ruled in Jerusalem for forty years. His mother Zibiah came from the southern town of Beersheba. God spared his life as an infant from a wicked queen, and now the young king began his long reign under godly care.

Joash lived in a way that pleased the Lord as long as the faithful priest Jehoiada was alive to guide him. The godly high priest taught the young king God's ways and kept the nation focused on true worship. Good mentors are a great blessing, but faith must also take root in a person's own heart.

Jehoiada selected two wives for Joash so that he could have sons and daughters. This helped rebuild the royal family of David, which had almost been wiped out by violence in earlier years. The godly priest acted like a loving father to guide the young king's home life.

When Joash grew older, he decided with all his heart to repair the Lord's temple. The temple of God in Jerusalem had been neglected and damaged during the rule of evil leaders. Joash wanted to honor God by restoring His holy house to beauty and safety.

Joash told the priests and Levites to travel through Judah and collect the annual temple tax from the people. He commanded them to hurry because the temple was in such bad shape. The Levites, however, dragged their feet and did not get the work done quickly.

Joash called for Jehoiada, the head of the priests, and asked why the Levites were delaying the collection. He reminded him of the regular tax Moses had commanded centuries earlier to support God's dwelling place. Joash wanted religious leaders to take responsibility for God's work.

The temple had fallen into ruin because the sons of the wicked Queen Athaliah had broken into it. They had even taken sacred items from the Lord's house and given them to the worship of the false god Baal. Wicked leadership had brought open shame and destruction upon God's holy place.

To solve the problem, the king ordered a large wooden chest to be made. They set it outside the entrance gate to the Lord's temple so everyone could see it. This gave the people an easy and safe way to put their money directly toward the repairs.

The king sent word across Judah and Jerusalem calling everyone to bring the tax that Moses had set up in the wilderness. Instead of waiting for collectors to visit them, the people were invited to bring their gifts straight to God's house. This reminded the nation of their shared duty to support the Lord's worship.

The leaders and the common people were filled with joy at this opportunity. They brought their offerings gladly and dropped them into the chest until it was filled. Giving to God's work is a delight when people give with willing, grateful hearts.

Whenever the chest became full, the Levites carried it to the king's royal accountants. The king's secretary and the chief priest's assistant emptied the box, counted the silver, and sent the chest back to its place. By repeating this process often, they gathered a huge amount of money with complete honesty.

The king and Jehoiada handed the silver over to the men supervising the temple repairs. These supervisors hired stonemasons, carpenters, and metalworkers who worked with iron and bronze. Everyone worked together with careful planning to restore the house of the Lord.

The craftsmen worked hard, and the repair work moved ahead steadily under their hands. They rebuilt the damaged sections and restored the temple to its original design and strength. When God's people unite in a good cause, great work can be completed.

After all the building repairs were done, the overseers brought the leftover money to the king and Jehoiada. With those extra funds, they made new gold and silver utensils and bowls for worship and sacrifice to replace what had been stolen. As long as Jehoiada lived, daily burnt offerings were faithfully presented to the Lord.

Jehoiada lived to an unusually old age and died at one hundred and thirty years old. His long life was a clear sign of God's favor and blessing on him. His death marked the end of a peaceful and faithful season for the nation of Judah.

The people gave Jehoiada the special honor of being buried among the kings in the City of David. They did this because he had served Israel so faithfully, restoring God's pure worship and caring for His temple. True honor comes to those who devote their lives to serving God and His people.

After Jehoiada died, the royal officials of Judah came and bowed down before King Joash, flattering him. They wanted permission to bring back false gods, and Joash weakly gave in to their wishes. Without his godly mentor, the king's lack of real conviction was revealed.

The leaders stopped worshipping at the Lord's temple and began serving wooden poles of the goddess Asherah and other idols. Their sudden turn against God brought His holy anger against Judah and Jerusalem. Leaving God's ways always leads to trouble and spiritual ruin.

Even in their rebellion, the Lord showed great mercy by sending prophets to warn them and call them back to Himself. These prophets spoke boldly against the nation's sins. Sadly, the king and the people shut their ears and refused to listen.

The Spirit of God came upon Zechariah, the son of the late priest Jehoiada. He stood on a raised platform above the crowd in the temple courts and warned them that breaking God's law would bring ruin. He told them plainly that because they had abandoned the Lord, the Lord had abandoned them.

The leaders formed a plot against Zechariah, and King Joash shockingly ordered his death. A mob stoned the prophet to death right in the courtyard of God's temple. It was a terrible crime to murder God's messenger in the very house of worship.

King Joash showed terrible ingratitude by murdering the son of Jehoiada, the man who had saved his life and made him king. As Zechariah was dying, he asked the Lord to see what happened and bring justice. God heard the dying martyr's plea and soon held the king accountable.

Before a year had passed, the army of Aram invaded Judah and reached Jerusalem. The invaders killed all the wicked officials who had led Joash into idol worship and sent the plunder home to Damascus. God used this foreign enemy to punish the very leaders who had turned away from Him.

The Aramean force had only a small number of soldiers, but the Lord handed a much larger Judean army over to them. Judah could not win because they had forsaken the Lord, the God of their ancestors. When people turn away from God, even large numbers cannot keep them safe.

When the Arameans withdrew, they left Joash wounded and suffering from terrible illness. Joash's own royal servants then plotted against him and killed him in his bed to avenge the murder of Jehoiada's son. He was buried in Jerusalem, but the people refused to give him a place in the royal tombs of the kings.

The conspirators who killed King Joash were Zabad and Jehozabad, two men whose mothers were from the foreign lands of Ammon and Moab. These palace servants struck down the king in his own bedroom. Joash had fallen so low that he was surrounded by foreign influences and betrayed by his own household.

The rest of the story of Joash, including his children, the prophetic warnings spoken against him, and his temple repairs, were recorded in an ancient commentary on the Book of the Kings. When he died, his son Amaziah became the next king. A life that started with great promise ended in tragic failure because of disobedience.
